findings.finding: KVM unconditionally grants guest VMs full CBIE=INV (cbo.inval with true invalidate semantics, ENVCFG_CBIE=0x3<<4=INV) when ZICBOM is available. Meanwhile, host userspace is deliberately restricted to only CBCFE (clean/flush) and cbo.inval is left as ILLEGAL (CBIE=00). The RISC-V spec explicitly warns (cmo.adoc:584-597) that granting lower-privilege software true invalidate capability 'may result in a security hole if lower privileged level software performs an invalidate operation and accesses sensitive information in memory.' The spec recommends either trapping cbo.inval or configuring it to perform a flush operation. KVM guests' VU-mode userspace thus has a cache-invalidate primitive that host userspace does not, violating the principle that a VM should not have capabilities exceeding its host process. The fix would be to either (a) set henvcfg.CBIE to FLUSH (01b) instead of INV (11b), making cbo.inval in guests perform a flush operation rather than true invalidate, or (b) gate the CBIE value on a user-configurable policy.

spec_citations.excerpt: A cbo.inval instruction executes or raises either an illegal-instruction exception or a virtual-instruction exception based on the state of the envcfg.CBIE fields... Until a modified cache block has updated memory, a cbo.inval instruction may expose stale data values in memory if the CSRs are programmed to perform an invalidate operation. This behavior may result in a security hole if lower privileged level software performs an invalidate operation and accesses sensitive information in memory. To avoid such holes, higher privileged level software must perform either a clean or flush operation on the cache block before permitting lower privileged level software to perform an invalidate operation on the block. Alternatively, higher privileged level software may program the CSRs so that cbo.inval either traps or performs a flush operation in a lower privileged level.

The Zicbom extension adds the CBIE WARL field to henvcfg. The CBIE field controls execution of the cache block invalidate instruction (CBO.INVAL) in privilege modes VS and VU... 01b -- The instruction is executed and performs a flush operation, even if configured by VS-mode to perform an invalidate operation. 11b -- The instruction is executed and performs an invalidate operation, unless configured by VS-mode to perform a flush operation.

findings.finding: Cross-hart CBO block size mismatch is only logged via pr_warn() but does not prevent boot. If one hart reports 64-byte blocks and another reports 128-byte blocks, tasks migrated between harts would use the first-discovered hart's block size for CBO operations on the destination hart. This could cause incomplete cache maintenance (flush only half a cache block) or incorrect zeroing (cbo.zero covering wrong range), leading to silent data corruption in DMA or clear_page paths. The pr_warn is insufficient; the kernel should either refuse to enable the mismatched extension or enforce the minimum common block size across all harts.

spec_citations.excerpt: norm:cache_block_size: The size of a cache block is implementation-defined. Software can discover the cache block size for CBO instructions through the execution environment discovery mechanism.
Software can discover the cache block size for each CBO instruction and the supported values of the CBIE field through the execution environment discovery mechanism.

findings.finding: Andes errata sets riscv_cbom_block_size = 1 with the comment 'Set this just to make core cbo code happy.' While 1 technically passes the is_power_of_2() check in riscv_ext_zicbom_validate() (since 2^0 = 1), it does not represent any real hardware cache block size. Using block_size=1 in ALT_CMO_OP loops means address masking with (size - 1) = 0, so block alignment is a no-op and every byte iteration emits a full CBO instruction. On hardware where actual cache blocks are 64 bytes, this causes 64x more CBO instructions than needed — severe performance degradation. More critically, if this value is ever used for cbo.zero via clear_page.S (which uses riscv_cboz_block_size, NOT riscv_cbom_block_size, so not directly affected), the incorrect alignment assumption could lead to memory corruption. The block_size=1 should be replaced with the actual Andes AX45MP cache line size (typically 64 bytes) discovered through the proper hardware probing mechanism.

spec_citations.excerpt: norm:cache_block_size: The size of a cache block is implementation-defined and must be discovered through the execution environment.

findings.finding: riscv_user_isa_enable() correctly enables only ENVCFG_CBCFE (cbo.clean/cbo.flush) and ENVCFG_CBZE (cbo.zero) for host userspace, while deliberately leaving CBIE at its reset value of ILLEGAL (00). This follows the RISC-V spec's security guidance (cmo.adoc:584-597) that cbo.inval should either trap or perform flush in lower privilege levels. Userspace can perform clean/flush/zero but cannot invalidate cache blocks. When any CMO extension is not available on all harts, a pr_warn is emitted and the extension is disabled globally — correct heterogeneous-SMP handling. Zicbop (prefetch) has no ENVCFG control bits, which is correct per the spec since prefetch instructions are 'may-be-operations' that never fault.

The context-switch path correctly saves and restores ENVCFG CSR on task switch via __switch_to_envcfg() at switch_to.h:124. The helper reads next->thread.envcfg and writes it to CSR_ENVCFG using an ALTERNATIVE that becomes NOP when XLINUXENVCFG is unavailable (e.g., on systems without the ENVCFG CSR). The envcfg_update_bits() helper at switch_to.h:73-82 also correctly handles immediate CSR write when modifying current's envcfg. Suspend/resume (suspend.h:16-48) independently saves/restores ENVCFG, which is correct because the suspend path bypasses normal context switch. Signal delivery does not need explicit ENVCFG save/restore because thread.envcfg persists across signals through the task_struct; a signal handler's any ENVCFG-modifying operation goes through envcfg_update_bits() which updates thread.envcfg directly.

KVM correctly uses csr_swap() to atomically exchange host SENVCFG with guest SENVCFG on vCPU load, and swaps back on vCPU put (kvm_riscv_vcpu_swap_in_host_state at vcpu.c:763-775). This ensures the host kernel's ENVCFG settings (including CBZE and CBCFE for userspace) are preserved while the guest runs, and the guest's own SENVCFG is in effect during guest execution. HENVCFG (the hypervisor-level control) is separately written in kvm_arch_vcpu_load() (vcpu.c:615/596) and governs whether guest CBO instructions are HS-qualified and at what privilege they execute. The SMSTATEEN0_HSENVCFG bit is also correctly set (vcpu.c:565) to allow guest access to HENVCFG when SMSTATEEN is implemented.

The ALT_CMO_OP macro correctly implements alternative-based CBO operations. When ZICBOM is available, it patches in a CBO loop (cbo.clean/flush/inval); when unavailable, it falls back to __nops(5), making the call a no-op. The no-op fallback is safe because: (a) arch_setup_dma_ops() at dma-noncoherent.c:139-141 already WARN_TAINTs when a non-coherent device is used without noncoherent support; (b) dma-noncoherent.c:148-151 additionally warns if riscv_noncoherent_supported() was called without a block size; (c) dma_cache_alignment is set to 1 when noncoherent is unsupported (dma-noncoherent.c:153-157), preventing incorrect alignment assumptions. The T-Head errata path (thead/errata.c:103-107) provides non-standard cache ops via a separate function pointer mechanism (riscv_nonstd_cache_ops) that is checked before ALT_CMO_OP in dma-noncoherent.c:22-28.
findings.snippet:
#define ALT_CMO_OP(_op, _start, _size, _cachesize)	\
asm volatile(ALTERNATIVE(				\
	__nops(5),					\
	"mv a0, %1\n\t"				\
	"j 2f\n\t"					\
	"3:\n\t"					\
	CBO_##_op(a0)					\
	...
	0, RISCV_ISA_EXT_ZICBOM, CONFIG_RISCV_ISA_ZICBOM)

findings.finding: signal.c has no explicit ENVCFG save/restore in the signal frame. This is compliant because ENVCFG is maintained as part of thread.envcfg in the task_struct and is restored by __switch_to_envcfg() on context switch (switch_to.h:124). A signal handler that modifies ENVCFG (e.g., via a prctl that calls envcfg_update_bits) writes to task->thread.envcfg, which persists correctly after signal return. The only risk would be if a signal handler directly executed CSRRW to ENVCFG — but userspace cannot write ENVCFG CSR directly (it's an S-mode CSR), so this is not possible. No signal-frame changes are needed.
findings.snippet: /* signal.c: no ENVCFG handling needed — thread.envcfg persists across signals */
